summary: Draw field lines with density proportional to magnitude, beginning and ending correctly, and never crossing.
objective: Make a field-line diagram carry the quantitative information the convention promises.
applies_when: An electrostatic field is drawn as continuous field lines rather than sampled arrows.
Charges, poles or sources of different strength appear together.
The viewer is expected to read relative field strength from the picture.
Another vector field, such as a magnetic or flow field, is drawn as lines and needs its own source rules, since it has no charge-like sources to begin and end on.
intent_signals: which region has a stronger field
why do the lines not cross
example_prompts: Draw field lines for two unequal charges with correct line counts.
Show where the field is strongest from the line spacing.
negative_signals: Sampled arrow grids, which follow different reading rules.
Decorative flow lines with no quantitative claim.
not_for: Sampled arrow grids, which follow different reading rules.
Decorative flow lines with no quantitative claim.

principles: Field-line density is the encoding: the line density at a point is proportional to the field magnitude there. That reading is quantitative only with a stated seeding and flux interpretation in a plane where it holds; apparent spacing in a projected three-dimensional view is not a magnitude measurement.

Field lines cannot cross in the field domain, because a crossing would give two directions at one point. That argument needs a non-zero, well-defined direction, so null points and singularities are genuine exceptions where lines may meet or terminate and need a stated policy. A crossing on screen is not evidence of a fault either: in a projected three-dimensional view, lines at different depths routinely appear to cross.

Lines begin on positive charges or come in from infinity and end on negative charges or continue to infinity, and the number attached to a charge is proportional to its magnitude, so unequal charges must not receive equal line counts.
Because the convention is quantitative, a hand-drawn or evenly spaced set of lines misinforms even when it looks tidy.
implementation: Seed lines in proportion to source magnitude rather than at a fixed count per source.

Integrate each line along the computed field with a step small enough to resolve strong gradients, and give termination an explicit policy: on a sink, at the domain boundary, at a null point, or on reaching a step limit, reporting which occurred.
Handle the neighbourhood of a singularity with a stated cutoff radius so integration does not produce spurious behaviour.
State the convention and the seeding rule in a legend, including whether the drawing is a section of a three-dimensional field.
In three dimensions, note that perceived spacing depends on projection, and consider a section or a magnitude encoding as a companion.
observable_checks: Test for intersections between line paths in the field domain rather than on screen, and expect apparent crossings in any projected view. Only require visually non-crossing lines in a true planar section of a field that lies in that plane.
Compare the number of lines on a source of double strength and confirm it is proportionally larger.
Compare line spacing between a strong and a weak region against the computed magnitudes.
Confirm every line ends according to the declared policy, and that lines approaching a null point are handled deliberately rather than wandering or stopping silently in empty space.

creative_affordances: Animated flow along the lines, colour by magnitude and stylised line rendering are all free choices.
A deliberately schematic diagram is fine when it is labelled as schematic rather than quantitative.
known_limits: Authored presentation guidance citing electrostatic field-line conventions; it does not extend to magnetic field lines or to fields with sources outside the domain.
Density reading in a three-dimensional projection is approximate and is not resolved by this rule.

claims.statement: In an electric field-line diagram the line density at a point is proportional to the magnitude of the field there, field lines can never cross because a line represents the field direction at a point, lines originate on positive charges or come in from infinity and terminate on negative charges or extend to infinity, and the number of lines at a charge is proportional to the magnitude of that charge.
claims.scope: Electrostatic field-line diagram conventions; magnetic field lines and other vector fields follow related but distinct conventions.
